genres.name: From the Indies to The Hague

place.name: Amsterdam, Royal Palace on Dam Square

genres.text: On 27 December 1949 the Netherlands transferred sovereignty to Indonesia in Amsterdam. In the years that followed, hundreds of thousands of Indo-Dutch people, with both Dutch and Indonesian roots, left for a country many of them had never seen. Many ended up in The Hague. Among them were young musicians who in the Indies had heard American rock 'n' roll, country, kroncong and Hawaiian guitar music. From that mixture indorock grew.

genres.name: Corry Brokken wins the Eurovision Song Contest
genres.text: On 3 March 1957 Corry Brokken won the second Eurovision Song Contest in Frankfurt with Net als toen, the first Dutch victory. In the song a woman sings about a love that has cooled. In those years the Song Contest was a major television event across Europe, and the Dutch-language song was very much in the spotlight. Two years later the Netherlands won again, with Teddy Scholten.
genres.listen: Listen to the orchestra and Brokken's clear, refined voice: Dutch-language music as it sounded on the radio in the 1950s.

genres.name: Tielman Brothers
genres.text: The brothers Andy, Reggy, Ponthon and Loulou Tielman came to the Netherlands with their family in 1957 and lived in Breda. They were one of the first bands to play rock 'n' roll here, with a show: Andy played guitar behind his head and the bass became an acrobat's prop. At the world's fair in Brussels in 1958 they drew a large audience. Later they became famous in Germany.
genres.listen: Listen to the fast, clear guitar lines with lots of echo. The echo unit is the sound of indorock.

genres.name: Peter Koelewijn: Kom van dat dak af
genres.text: On 8 January 1960 Kom van dat dak af by Peter en zijn Rockets, the band of Peter Koelewijn from Eindhoven, was released. It is regarded as the first Dutch-language rock 'n' roll record. Koelewijn took his example from Chuck Berry and Little Richard. Radio presenter Co de Kloet played the song three times in one broadcast of Tijd voor Teenagers, and it became a number 1 hit. Rock in their own language turned out to be possible.
genres.listen: Listen to the driving boogie-woogie piano and the Dutch lyrics that move as fast as American rock 'n' roll.

tracks.artist: Peter Koelewijn en zijn Rockets & Peter Koelewijn
tracks.title: Kom van dat dak af

genres.name: Radio Veronica
genres.text: In May 1960 Radio Veronica began broadcasting from a ship off the coast at Scheveningen, outside Dutch law. The regular broadcasters played little pop music, Veronica played it all day. From 1965 the station had its own chart, the Top 40. For young people Veronica became the place where they heard new music. In 1974 the station had to stop, and shortly afterwards Veronica continued as a public broadcaster.

genres.name: The Blue Diamonds: Ramona
genres.text: In 1960 the Indo-Dutch brothers Riem and Ruud de Wolff, as The Blue Diamonds, had a big hit with Ramona, an old American song that they sang in two-part harmony, with soft guitars. In Germany it reached number one. It was one of the first big international successes of Dutch pop musicians. Indo-Dutch musicians were the first to show that Dutch people could make pop music for the world.
genres.listen: Listen to how the two brothers sing together exactly, in thirds, like the Everly Brothers in America.

genres.name: The Golden Earrings begin in The Hague
genres.text: In 1961 the boys George Kooymans, then 13, and Rinus Gerritsen, then 15, from The Hague decided to start a band. They called themselves The Golden Earrings, after a song by the band The Hunters from The Hague. Thanks to indorock, The Hague was the guitar capital of the Netherlands. In 1965 they scored their first top 10 hit with Please Go. As Golden Earring they would keep playing for sixty years, until 2021.
genres.listen: Listen to the English lyrics and the jangling guitars: this is how Nederbeat sounded, Dutch beat music modelled on British examples.

genres.name: Two times nul points at Eurovision
genres.text: On 18 March 1962 De Spelbrekers sang the cheerful Katinka at the Song Contest in Luxembourg. They received not a single point and finished at the bottom together with three other countries. A year later, on 23 March 1963 in London, the same happened to Annie Palmen with Een speeldoos. After the victories of 1957 and 1959, the Dutch song turned out not to win in Europe by itself.
genres.listen: Listen to the light, neat little song with close harmony, in which two voices sing close together, as it sounded on the radio in the early 1960s.

genres.name: Anneke Grönloh: Brandend zand
genres.text: In July 1962 Brandend zand by Anneke Grönloh was released. She was born in 1942 in Tondano in the Dutch East Indies and spent her first years in a Japanese internment camp. The song is a translation by Johnny Hoes of the German Heißer Sand. It stayed at the top of the charts for weeks and is said to have sold more than three million copies worldwide. In 2000 Grönloh was named singer of the century.
genres.listen: Listen to the exotic atmosphere of desert and longing, and Grönloh's warm, powerful voice.

genres.name: The Rolling Stones at the Kurhaus
genres.text: On 8 August 1964 the Rolling Stones played at the Kurhaus in Scheveningen. After only a few songs it went wrong: young people fought, tore up chairs and stormed the stage. After less than a quarter of an hour the band had to stop and flee. It was their first gig in the Netherlands. Newspapers wrote in shock about the youth. The riot showed how strongly beat music affected young people in the Netherlands.

genres.name: The Top 40
genres.text: On 2 January 1965 Radio Veronica broadcast the first Top 40, devised by DJ Joost den Draaijer. Every week the forty best-selling singles in the Netherlands were put in a row. Record shops put up the list, and young people followed who was rising and falling. The Top 40 still exists and is one of the oldest charts in Europe. Whether a Dutch record got into it often decided its success.

genres.name: Boudewijn de Groot: Welterusten mijnheer de president
genres.text: In 1966 Boudewijn de Groot sang Welterusten mijnheer de president, a mocking lullaby to the American president Johnson about the war in Vietnam. The lyrics were written by Lennaert Nijgh. It was Bob Dylan, Dutch style: a protest song in their own language, with an acoustic guitar. De Groot and Nijgh showed that in Dutch you could make serious songs that appealed to young people.
genres.listen: Listen to the soft, rocking melody, like a lullaby, beneath a sharp lyric about bombs and war.

genres.name: Q65 and Nederbeat
genres.text: In 1966 the band Q65 from The Hague and the Outsiders from Amsterdam had their first hits. They played raw, English-language beat music, rougher than many British examples. The Hague became the beat city of the Netherlands, with dozens of bands. In Amsterdam the youth magazine Hitweek wrote about this music. The press spoke of Nederbeat. The bands remained little known outside the Netherlands, but later collectors all over the world went looking for these records.
genres.listen: The Life I Live by Q65 is raw and loud, with a screaming singer and a guitar that grates.

genres.name: The Cats and the palingsound
genres.text: In 1968 The Cats from the fishing village of Volendam reached number 1 for the first time with Lea. Singer Piet Veerman had taken the lead that year. Radio Veronica DJ Joost den Draaijer called their soft, multi-voiced sound the palingsound (eel sound), after the eel for which Volendam is known. After The Cats came BZN, Jan Smit and Nick & Simon. In this way one village became a musical style of its own.
genres.listen: Listen to the soft harmony singing and the melancholy melody: the typical sound of the palingsound.

genres.name: Ramses Shaffy and Liesbeth List: Pastorale
genres.text: In 1964 the actor Ramses Shaffy started a cabaret group of his own, Shaffy Chantant, with the singer Liesbeth List. In 1967 he received a gold record for Sammy. In 1968 Shaffy and List recorded Pastorale together, a restrained duet about love and hope. For years afterwards they toured the Netherlands and Flanders. Chanson and theatre thus came together in songs that whole halls sang along to.
genres.listen: Listen to how two voices take turns and softly come together. It is almost a conversation, with little accompaniment around it.

genres.name: Herman van Veen: Waar blijft de tijd
genres.text: In 1965 the violinist Herman van Veen from Utrecht stood on stage for the first time with Harlekijn, a musical programme full of clowning. In 1968 his first album followed, with Waar blijft de tijd, a Dutch version of a song by Jean Ferrat. A year later he received the Zilveren Harp, a Dutch music prize. After that he performed his shows in five languages, all over the world.
genres.listen: Listen to Van Veen's clear voice and the violin or acoustic ensemble beneath it. Notice how calmly and narratively he sings.

genres.name: Lenny Kuhr: De troubadour
genres.text: On 29 March 1969 the nineteen-year-old Lenny Kuhr won the Song Contest in Madrid with De troubadour, together with three other countries, which all had the same number of points. She had co-written the song herself and sang it with her guitar, as a modern singer-songwriter. De troubadour is about a medieval singer who travels from town to town. It was the third Dutch victory.
genres.listen: Listen to how the song begins with only guitar and voice, and then grows bigger with an orchestra.

genres.name: Cuby + Blizzards in Grolloo
genres.text: Not all Nederbeat came from the Randstad, the urban west of the country. Cuby + Blizzards worked from Grolloo, a small village in Drenthe. Singer Harry Muskee and guitarist Eelco Gelling played blues: not the cheerful beat of the Beatles, but the heavy music of the American South. They even accompanied bluesmen such as John Mayall and Van Morrison on tour. In 1969 their album Appleknockers Flophouse was released.
genres.listen: On Appleknockers Flophouse you hear a Hammond organ, a dark voice and a guitar that takes its time. Raw and English-language.

genres.name: George Baker Selection: Little Green Bag
genres.text: In 1969 the George Baker Selection from the Zaanstreek had a hit with Little Green Bag, in 1970 in America too. Singer Hans Bouwens performed as George Baker. The song begins with a famous bass line. In 1992 the director Quentin Tarantino used it in the film Reservoir Dogs, and so a new generation heard it. In those years Dutch pop music crossed the border mainly in English.
genres.listen: Listen to the bass line and the drums at the beginning: a few bars that later became famous in an American film.

genres.name: Shocking Blue: Venus
genres.text: On 7 February 1970 Venus by the band Shocking Blue from The Hague was number one in America, the first Dutch number one there. Guitarist Robbie van Leeuwen wrote it, Mariska Veres sang. But what is Dutch about Venus? Not the language, not the style either: only the musicians and the city. To an American listener it was simply a pop song. That question runs through the whole history of Nederpop.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar riff at the beginning and the low voice of Mariska Veres, with a slight accent in her English.

genres.name: Pinkpop
genres.text: On Whit Monday, 18 May 1970, the first Pinkpop was held in Geleen in Limburg, with Dutch and foreign bands. The festival was repeated every year and grew into the oldest annual pop festival in the world that still exists. In June 1970 the big festival in Kralingen near Rotterdam followed. For Dutch bands, festivals became a place to grow big.

genres.name: Toppop
genres.text: On 22 September 1970 the AVRO began Toppop, a television programme with pop music, presented by Ad Visser. Artists mimed in the studio, and the Toppop Ballet danced along. In this way young Dutch people saw their favourites every week, including well-known foreign artists. Toppop also made clips itself. The programme ran until 1988, when videos and MTV took over the job.

genres.name: Focus: Hocus Pocus
genres.text: In 1971 Hocus Pocus by Focus was released, the band of organist and flautist Thijs van Leer and guitarist Jan Akkerman. Both were technically strong musicians, but their best-known song became a joke: a hard guitar riff, a drum break, yodelling, whistling and a flute solo. In 1973 it became a hit in England and America. Prog rock with humour: English bands hardly dared to do that.
genres.listen: Count the parts: riff, drum break, yodelling and flute solo. Just try playing it yourself.

genres.name: Golden Earring: Radar Love
genres.text: In 1973 Radar Love by Golden Earring from The Hague was released, a rock song about a man driving to his lover at night. It became a hit in England and America and is one of the best-known rock songs for the car. Golden Earring existed from 1961 to 2021, one of the longest-running rock bands in the world. The band stopped when guitarist George Kooymans contracted the disease ALS.
genres.listen: The bass and the drums hit the motorway: the groove is the song. Also listen to the drum solo in the middle.

genres.name: Wim Sonneveld: Het dorp
genres.text: In 1974 Het dorp by the cabaret artist Wim Sonneveld was released, shortly after his death. It is an adaptation of La montagne by the French chansonnier Jean Ferrat. The Dutch lyrics are by Friso Wiegersma. The song is about a village that progress has changed beyond recognition. The Dutch-language songs of those years came more from Paris than from Liverpool. Het dorp has been high in the Top 2000 for years.
genres.listen: Listen to how Sonneveld tells the song more than he sings it, like a chansonnier, with nostalgia for a vanished world.

genres.name: Teach-In: Ding-a-dong
genres.text: On 22 March 1975 Teach-In from Enschede won the Song Contest in Stockholm with Ding-a-dong, sung by Getty Kaspers. It was the fourth Dutch victory, and for a long time the last. The cheerful song also became a hit outside the Netherlands, including in England, just like ABBA a year earlier with Waterloo. After that it took 44 years before the Netherlands won again.
genres.listen: Ding-a-dong is a skipping pop song with a chorus that you can sing along to in any language.

genres.name: Normaal: Oerend hard
genres.text: In 1977 Normaal from the Achterhoek had a hit with Oerend hard, about two drunk motorcyclists and an accident, sung in the Achterhoeks dialect. It was probably the first hit in a regional language. The band around singer Bennie Jolink was formed in 1974 and played raw farmers' rock, in clogs and overalls. Dialect was the language of an identity of their own, of a region that would not let Amsterdam or Hilversum speak for it.
genres.listen: Put Oerend hard next to Radar Love: two rock songs about the road that nobody would confuse with each other.

genres.name: Herman Brood: Saturday Night
genres.text: In 1978 Herman Brood had a hit with his band Wild Romance with Saturday Night. Brood was a pianist, painter and the first real rock 'n' roll star of the Netherlands, who openly lived the way he sang, with drugs and scandals. In 1979 he tried to conquer America, without much success. His lifestyle eventually proved fatal: in 2001 he jumped from the roof of the Hilton in Amsterdam.
genres.listen: Saturday Night is raw rock 'n' roll with piano. Listen to Brood's hoarse voice and the driving guitars.

genres.name: Massada at Pinkpop
genres.text: On 4 June 1979 Massada played at Pinkpop in Geleen, on the same day as The Police and Dire Straits. Massada was a Dutch-Moluccan band from Huizen that at first played mainly at Moluccan parties. The band mixed rock with Latin American rhythms and plenty of percussion, like Santana. With hits such as Arumbai and Sajang é they brought Moluccan music and language into the Dutch charts.
genres.listen: Listen to the many drums and the Moluccan lyrics above a danceable Latin rhythm.

genres.name: Doe Maar and the switch of language
genres.text: In 1981 Doe Maar entered the charts, with ska and reggae in Dutch. In Sinds 1 dag of 2 (32 jaar) Henny Vrienten sings about a man of 32 who is in love again. With Doris Day the breakthrough followed in 1982, and the Doe Maar craze: screaming fans and posters. For the first time a Dutch-language pop group was at the centre of a youth culture. In 1984 the band stopped.
genres.listen: Listen to the ska rhythm on the offbeat. A Dutch-language pop song that does not sound old-fashioned or small-town.

genres.name: Het Goede Doel: België
genres.text: In 1982 Het Goede Doel, the band from Utrecht around Henk Westbroek and Henk Temming, had a hit with België, synthpop in Dutch. The chorus consists of questions that seem to be about nothing. After Doe Maar, dozens of Dutch-language bands followed within a few years. That is how Nederpop arose in the sense the word usually has now: Dutch pop music in their own language.
genres.listen: Listen to the synthesizers and the cool vocals, with a chorus full of questions.

genres.name: Vandenberg: Burning Heart
genres.text: In 1982 Burning Heart was released by the band of guitarist Adrian Vandenberg. It is a power ballad: a quiet beginning, a big chorus and a guitar solo building to a climax. It became a hit in the United States. Vandenberg made hard rock that sounded exactly the way American rock radio wanted. Later he became the guitarist of the British band Whitesnake. Nothing Dutch could be heard in Burning Heart, and that was the intention.
genres.listen: Listen to how the power ballad is built: quiet beginning, big chorus and a guitar solo that lifts the song.

genres.name: Klein Orkest: Over de muur
genres.text: In 1984 Over de muur by Klein Orkest became a hit. Singer and lyricist Harrie Jekkers came from cabaret. The song is about East and West Berlin and asks whether life in the West is really so much freer than in the East. That was not an obvious question then. Five years later the Wall fell. Here kleinkunst and pop come together: a story song with a chorus that everyone sings along to.
genres.listen: Listen to how Jekkers tells the story, with a comparison between East and West, and a chorus to sing along to.

genres.name: Frank Boeijen Groep: Zwart wit
genres.text: On 21 August 1983 the fifteen-year-old Kerwin Duinmeijer was stabbed to death in Amsterdam because he was black. Frank Boeijen wrote Zwart wit about it, which became a hit in 1984. It is new wave in Dutch, with cool guitars and synthesizers. Boeijen showed that a pop song in their own language could also be about a racist murder in their own country.
genres.listen: Listen to the cool guitars and the detached vocals beneath a lyric that asks how something like this can happen.

genres.name: De Dijk: Mag het licht uit
genres.text: In 1987 Mag het licht uit by De Dijk from Amsterdam was released. The band chose American soul and rhythm and blues as its source, with horns and a tight rhythm section. Singer Huub van der Lubbe wrote lyrics about Amsterdam and the people who live there. De Dijk became one of the most popular live acts in the country. In 2010 the band even recorded an album with the American soul singer Solomon Burke.
genres.listen: Listen to the horns and the warmth of a soul ballad, with Huub van der Lubbe as the singer of the city.

genres.name: The Scene: Iedereen is van de wereld
genres.text: In 1990 Iedereen is van de wereld was released by The Scene, the band of singer Thé Lau. The chorus has the simplicity of an anthem. It got no further than the Tipparade, the chart for new songs, but grew into a regular singalong at festivals and has been in the Top 2000 every year since 1999. Thé Lau died in 2015. A song can also become important slowly.
genres.listen: Listen to the solid guitar rock and the chorus that sounds like an anthem.

genres.name: Osdorp Posse
genres.text: Around 1990 Osdorp Posse from the Amsterdam district of Osdorp began rapping in Dutch. Rapper Def P did not choose refined Dutch, but coarse Amsterdam speech: raw, angry and crude, with heavy beats. That is how Nederhop arose. In hip-hop Osdorp Posse did what Normaal had done in rock: the music came from America, but the language and the attitude were from here.
genres.listen: Listen to the hard beat and Def P's coarse Amsterdam speech. Not an American imitation, but a voice of their own.

genres.name: Rowwen Hèze: Bestel mar
genres.text: Rowwen Hèze came from the small Limburg village of America and sang in the dialect of North Limburg. Their music was a mixture of rock, polka, Tex-Mex and Irish folk, with an accordion. Bestel mar from 1991 became a singalong at every party and festival in the south. Like Normaal, they showed that music from the region could draw a large audience, far beyond their own area.
genres.listen: Bestel mar is a cheerful drinking song. Listen to the accordion and the Limburg dialect.

genres.name: Gabber and Thunderdome
genres.text: In the early 1990s DJs and producers in Rotterdam made house harder and faster: gabber, with more than 150 beats per minute and a distorted bass drum. It came with a youth culture of its own, with shaved heads and tracksuits. In 1992 ID&T organised the first Thunderdome party. Gabber was the first Dutch dance music to become known abroad as something typically Dutch.
genres.listen: Poing by Rotterdam Termination Source became a hit in 1992. Listen to the bouncing sounds above a bass drum that hits like a hammer.

genres.name: 2 Unlimited: No Limit
genres.text: In the spring of 1993 No Limit by 2 Unlimited was number one in more than 35 countries. The face of the group was Dutch: rapper Ray Slijngaard and singer Anita Doth. The music came from the Belgian producers Phil Wilde and Jean-Paul De Coster. It was the biggest international success of Dutch pop musicians in years, and the song had almost no lyrics.
genres.listen: Count the parts: synth riff, rap, chorus and break. In the British version the rap is cut out, except for the word techno.

genres.name: Marco Borsato: Dromen zijn bedrog
genres.text: In 1994 Marco Borsato had an enormous hit with Dromen zijn bedrog, a Dutch version of an Italian song. It stayed at number one for weeks. Borsato became the best-selling Dutch singer of his time, with big ballads in Dutch and sold-out stadium concerts. Critics found his music slick, but he showed how large the audience for the Dutch-language song was.
genres.listen: Listen to the big ballad with strings and a chorus that keeps climbing. Made to sing along to loudly.

genres.name: Extince: Spraakwater
genres.text: In 1995 Extince from Oosterhout in Brabant had a top 10 hit with Spraakwater, with samples from De Fabeltjeskrant. It was the first Dutch-language hip-hop record to become a big hit. Extince rapped playfully and with pride in Dutch, and showed that the language rhymes perfectly well. After the raw Amsterdam speech of Osdorp Posse, a more cheerful side was now added. More and more young people began rapping in Dutch themselves.
genres.listen: At the beginning, listen for the voice of Meneer de Uil from De Fabeltjeskrant, and then for how Extince plays with the sound of the Dutch words.

genres.name: Skik: Op fietse
genres.text: In 1997 Op fietse by Skik was released, the band of Daniël Lohues from Drenthe, sung in the Drents dialect. The song describes a bicycle ride through the south-east of Drenthe, where Lohues grew up. Lohues sang about ordinary country life, without exaggeration. After Normaal and Rowwen Hèze, Skik showed that even a quiet song in dialect could be played all over the Netherlands.
genres.listen: Listen to the relaxed guitar pop and the Drents dialect, like a bike ride on a summer's day.

genres.name: Acda en de Munnik: Het regent zonnestralen
genres.text: In 1998 Het regent zonnestralen by Acda en de Munnik was released, the duo of Thomas Acda and Paul de Munnik. They came from the theatre and played in theatres, with guitars and piano, personal songs with lyrics you had to be able to follow. Here the line continues that began with kleinkunst and Boudewijn de Groot: singable songs, with a guitar, in their own language.
genres.listen: Listen to the acoustic guitars and the two voices that take turns in a personal song.

genres.name: Heideroosjes
genres.text: In 1999 the single Iedereen is gek (behalve jij)! was released by the Heideroosjes from Horst in Limburg. The band played punk: short, hard and fast, in English and in Dutch, with plenty of humour. They also toured Europe. So within twenty years almost every rock genre had acquired a Dutch-language variant: from the story song of Klein Orkest to the soul of De Dijk and the punk of the Heideroosjes.
genres.listen: Listen to how fast and short the song is, with a lyric that does not take itself too seriously.

genres.name: The first Top 2000
genres.text: On Boxing Day 1999 Radio 2 began the Top 2000, a list of the two thousand favourite songs of all time, chosen by listeners. It was meant as a one-off programme for the turn of the century, but it became an annual tradition between Christmas and New Year. Dutch songs such as Avond by Boudewijn de Groot and Het dorp by Wim Sonneveld are in it every year.

genres.name: Doe Maar back at Ahoy
genres.text: On 22 April 2000 Klaar was released, the first new album by Doe Maar since the band stopped in 1984. It entered at number 1 straight away. The band gave sixteen concerts at Rotterdam Ahoy for more than 175,000 visitors. Sixteen years after the farewell, the love for the band proved just as great. It showed how deeply rooted Dutch-language pop had become by then.
genres.listen: Listen to the familiar voices of Henny Vrienten and Ernst Jansz, singing about a love that is over.

genres.name: Twarres: Wêr bisto
genres.text: In 2000 Wêr bisto was released, by the duo Twarres from the Frisian village of Warga. The song, Frisian for Where are you, became a number 1 hit in the Netherlands and in Flanders. To date it is the only Frisian-language number 1 hit in the Netherlands. A year earlier the duo had won the audience prize with it at Liet, a song contest for songs in regional languages.
genres.listen: Listen to Mirjam Timmer's clear voice and see whether you can follow the Frisian.

genres.name: The first Sensation
genres.text: In 2000 ID&T, the company behind Thunderdome, organised a big dance party in the Amsterdam ArenA: Sensation. A year later came the famous dress code: everyone in white, in honour of the late brother of organiser Duncan Stutterheim. Sensation grew into an export product held in dozens of countries. It showed that the Netherlands could make big dance parties for a stadium full of people.

genres.name: Armin van Buuren: A State of Trance
genres.text: On 18 May 2001 ID&T Radio broadcast the first episode of A State of Trance, the radio programme of DJ Armin van Buuren from Leiden. Every week he mixed two hours of new trance, dance music with long build-ups and floating melodies. The programme grew into one of the biggest DJ shows in the world, with tens of millions of listeners in more than eighty countries.
genres.listen: Listen to how the track slowly builds up with floating synthesizers and a voice that keeps returning.

genres.name: Within Temptation: Ice Queen
genres.text: In January 2002 Ice Queen by Within Temptation from Waddinxveen became a big hit. That was because fans asked in huge numbers for the clip on the music channel The Box. The band makes symphonic metal: heavy guitars combined with orchestral sounds and the clear voice of Sharon den Adel. Within Temptation became popular mainly in Germany and beyond, and is among the most successful bands in that genre.
genres.listen: Listen to the contrast between the heavy guitars and Sharon den Adel's light, almost classical singing voice.

genres.name: Brainpower: Dansplaat
genres.text: In May 2002 the Amsterdam rapper Brainpower released Dansplaat. The song stayed at number 1 in the Top 40 for four weeks and was also top in Flanders. Brainpower was the first Dutch-language solo rapper to reach number 1 in both countries. In the lyrics he names all sorts of things from that time, from Wim Kok to Tekken 3. Nederhop had thus truly become pop music.
genres.listen: Listen to the fast, playful raps and notice the references to names and things from 2002.

genres.name: Defqon.1 and hardstyle
genres.text: In 2003 the organiser Q-dance held the first edition of Defqon.1 on the beach at Almere. The festival centred on hardstyle, a fast, hard dance style that came out of the gabber of the 1990s. Every year Defqon.1 got an anthem of its own, a song made especially for the festival. Later it moved to Biddinghuizen and drew visitors from all over the world.
genres.listen: Listen to the distorted, hard bass drum and the festive melody: this is what a hardstyle anthem sounds like, in this case the one for Defqon.1 in 2009.

genres.name: Tiësto at the Olympic Games
genres.text: On 13 August 2004 the Dutch DJ Tiësto played at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens, while the athletes walked into the stadium. It was the first time a DJ was given such a place. For years Tiësto was voted best DJ in the world. Notably, the biggest international success of Dutch pop music in those years was music without Dutch lyrics, often without any lyrics at all.
genres.listen: Tiësto's version of Adagio for Strings turns a sad classical piece by Samuel Barber into trance, with a rousing beat.

genres.name: Farewell to André Hazes
genres.text: On 23 September 2004 the folk singer André Hazes died. Four days later about 48,000 people said goodbye to him in the Amsterdam ArenA, and some six million viewers followed it on television. Hazes sang levensliedjes: sensitive songs about love, sorrow and ordinary life. After his death Zij gelooft in mij was released again and reached number 1 for the first time.
genres.listen: Listen to Hazes's raw, emotional voice and the simple melody that anyone can sing along to.

genres.name: Lange Frans & Baas B: Zinloos
genres.text: On 5 October 2004 Zinloos by Lange Frans & Baas B was released, with singer Ninthe in the chorus. The song protests against senseless violence, violence without any cause, and names victims such as Meindert Tjoelker. It stayed at number 1 in the Top 40 for three weeks. In this way Nederhop showed that rap could also be about social issues that touched the whole Netherlands.
genres.listen: Listen to the contrast between the narrative raps in the verses and Ninthe's sung, sad chorus.

genres.name: The first Serious Request
genres.text: From 20 to 24 December 2004 the 3FM DJs Giel Beelen, Claudia de Breij and Wouter van der Goes sat in a Glazen Huis (Glass House) on the Neude in Utrecht. They ate nothing and made radio day and night. Listeners paid money to request a record. In this way Serious Request raised almost a million euros for the Red Cross, for aid in Darfur.

genres.name: De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig: Watskeburt?!
genres.text: In 2005 Watskeburt?! was released, the first hit of De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig from Amsterdam. The song stayed at number one in the Top 40 for three weeks. The group turned language into a playground, with invented words, street slang, absurd jokes and electronic beats. They knew the word watskeburt from Amsterdam street slang. After 2000 Nederhop grew into one of the most important genres in the country.

genres.name: Daniël Lohues: Allennig
genres.text: On 27 March 2006 Allennig was released, the first solo album by Daniël Lohues, known from the band Skik. Allennig is Drents for alone: Lohues sings in his own regional language, quietly and personally. More volumes followed, and Allennig II reached the top 15 of the album chart in 2008. Lohues showed that a regional language is also suited to quiet, personal songs.
genres.listen: Listen to Lohues's quiet voice and try to follow the Drents lyrics.

genres.name: Concert at SEA
genres.text: On 30 June 2006 the band BLØF from Zeeland organised Concert at SEA for the first time, a festival on the Brouwersdam, between the North Sea and the Grevelingenmeer. From 2008 it lasted two days, with about 40,000 visitors a day, mainly for Dutch artists. It showed how large the audience for Dutch-language pop music had become. BLØF itself, formed in 1992 in Vlissingen, makes pop songs from Zeeland.

genres.name: Afrojack: Take Over Control
genres.text: In August 2010 DJ Afrojack from Spijkenisse released Take Over Control, with singer Eva Simons. The song became a hit in the Netherlands and also reached the British Top 40. A few months later Afrojack won a Grammy together with David Guetta for a remix of Madonna. Around 2010 Dutch DJs like him became world stars in popular EDM, electronic dance music.
genres.listen: Listen to the build-up to the drop, the moment when the beat and the sharp synthesizers suddenly come back in full.

genres.name: Gers Pardoel: Ik neem je mee
genres.text: On 17 October 2011 Ik neem je mee was released by the rapper Gers Pardoel from Nijmegen. The cheerful love song spent a total of six weeks at number 1 in the Top 40. In 2012 it became the most successful Dutch-language hit ever in the Top 40, a record that was only broken in 2023. Rap in their own language now belonged entirely in the ordinary hit parade.
genres.listen: Listen to how Gers raps and sings at the same time, over a sunny, simple guitar beat.

genres.name: Martin Garrix: Animals
genres.text: In June 2013 Animals was released by the seventeen-year-old Martin Garrix from Amstelveen. The song became a hit across Europe and a fixture at festivals. Garrix had made it at home, in his bedroom studio. In the same year Hardwell was voted best DJ in the world. With Tiësto, Armin van Buuren and Afrojack, Dutch producers defined a large part of dance music.
genres.listen: Animals has almost no vocals. Listen to the drop: a bare, hard synthesizer riff above a stomping beat.

genres.name: Typhoon: Hemel valt
genres.text: In 2014 the album Lobi da basi was released by Typhoon, the artist name of Glenn de Randamie. He grew up in 't Harde and began rapping in Zwolle, where a hip-hop scene of its own had arisen around the group Opgezwolle. On Hemel valt Typhoon combines hip-hop with soul and jazz. The album won an Edison. In Nederhop the sound, the rhyme and the street slang count just as heavily as the beat.
genres.listen: Listen to how hip-hop, soul and jazz flow into each other, with Typhoon's rap running cheerfully and fast over the beat.

genres.name: Nederhop on Spotify
genres.text: Since February 2014 streams have counted towards the Top 40, and after that the chart changed. Dutch rappers such as Lil Kleine, Ronnie Flex, Boef and Frenna were played little on the radio, but young people streamed them in huge numbers. In 2015 Drank & Drugs by Lil Kleine and Ronnie Flex was number one. Streaming showed what people really listened to, and that often turned out to be Dutch-language.
genres.listen: Krantenwijk by Lil Kleine and Boef from 2017 became big mainly through streams. Listen to the calm beat and how the rappers take turns telling about the past.

genres.name: BLØF: Zoutelande
genres.text: In 2017 BLØF had a big hit with Zoutelande, a duet with the Flemish singer Geike Arnaert about a beach in Zeeland. The song was a Dutch adaptation of a German song. It was at number one for weeks and for years remained one of the most streamed Dutch-language songs. The little village of Zoutelande suddenly got a lot of extra tourists.
genres.listen: Listen to how the two voices take turns, the Zeeland one and the Flemish one, over a calm, summery beat.

genres.name: Duncan Laurence: Arcade
genres.text: On 18 May 2019 Duncan Laurence won the Song Contest in Tel Aviv with Arcade, the first Dutch victory since 1975. Two years later the song became popular again through TikTok, now outside Europe as well. In 2021 it entered the American chart and became one of the most streamed Song Contest songs ever. In 2020 the Netherlands was due to host the contest, but it was cancelled because of corona.
genres.listen: Arcade begins with only piano and a soft voice. Listen to how the chorus keeps getting bigger, with a choir in the background.

genres.name: Snelle: Smoorverliefd
genres.text: In 2020 Snelle from Deventer had a number 1 hit with Smoorverliefd, a love song that was part of a campaign against phone use while cycling. Snelle began as a rapper and increasingly turned to singing. He released his first records on his own label. Anyone who used to want to get on the radio had to go through label bosses and DJs. A new generation also found its audience through streaming and social media.
genres.listen: Listen to the simple guitar and the rap that turns into singing. A rapper who makes pop songs.

genres.name: Golden Earring stops
genres.text: In February 2021 Golden Earring announced it was stopping, after sixty years. Guitarist George Kooymans had been diagnosed with ALS. The band began in The Hague in 1961 as The Golden Earrings, and between 1965 and 2003 had dozens of hits in the Top 40, including Radar Love and Twilight Zone. That made it one of the longest-running rock bands in the world, and the best-known Dutch rock export.

genres.name: Froukje: Groter dan ik
genres.text: In 2021 Froukje Veenstra broke through with electropop in Dutch. Groter dan ik is about climate anxiety: the feeling that the world's problems are too big for one person. Put it next to Welterusten mijnheer de president: Boudewijn de Groot sang about Vietnam in 1966, Froukje sings about the future of the planet. Both in their own language, for an audience of their own age.
genres.listen: Listen to the electronic beat and the soft voice beneath a lyric about something too big to carry.

genres.name: Joost Klein: Europapa
genres.text: In March 2024 Europapa by Joost Klein from Friesland became a hit on TikTok and Spotify, at number one in the Netherlands and Flanders. The cheerful, chaotic song is about travelling freely through Europe, and also about his late father. After an incident behind the scenes, Joost was removed from the contest on 11 May, the day of the final in Malmö. The song remained popular afterwards.
genres.listen: Europapa sounds like a gabber party with a childlike chorus. Joost sings in Dutch and raps about the countries of Europe.
